paragraph: The hostile kings of Haihayas, Telanghas and Sasibindus, rose against Aista and exiled him from his kingdom. King Aista with his counselors reached Bhriguprasravana at which time both his queens were without child. The story goes that when one of them was pregnant, the other with the intent of destroying the embryo poisoned her. The queen who had been poisoned approached and paid obeisance to venerable sage Bhargava Chyavana, who was then residing in that region. He told her, that she would soon give birth to an auspicious and virtuous son of great valor and of glory". "Soon after a charming child was born and because it was born with poison, he came to be known as Sagara. From him came Asamanjasa and Anshuman. Then came Dilipa, Bhagiratha, Kakutstha, Raghu, and Pravriddha. Pravriddha begot Purushadaka who begot Shamkhana, whose son was Sudarshana and the line went on, with Agnivarna, Sighraga, Maru, Ambarish, Nahusha, Yayati, Nabhaga and Aja. From Aja was born Dasaratha and Dasaratha begot Rama and Lakshmana. This is the genealogy of the dynasty, a dynasty of great monarchs, full of virtue and valor. Their passion for truth and for righteousness is renowned. I now request you to give your two daughters in marriage to the two Ikshvaku princes".
Chapter/Canto/Verse_Reference: Bala Kanda, Sarga 70 (Vasishta Narrates Ikshvaku Genealogy)
Characters_Involved: Sagara (and subsequent generations including Dasaratha, Rama, Lakshmana)
Situation/Problem_Faced: Vasishta, at Dasaratha's behest, narrates the elaborate genealogy of the Ikshvaku dynasty. This includes a dramatic story of one of King Aista's queens being poisoned by another, leading to the miraculous birth of Sagara with the help of Sage Chyavana. The narration formally presents the lineage of Rama and Lakshmana to Janaka, leading to the request for his daughters' hands in marriage.
Key_Teaching/Action_Taken: This passage establishes the illustrious and virtuous lineage of Rama and Lakshmana, highlighting their descent from a line of powerful, righteous, and valorous kings. It underscores the importance of ancestry and purity of lineage in royal marriages. The dramatic story of Sagara's birth emphasizes divine intervention and the overcoming of adversity within the dynasty's history. The formal presentation of the genealogy is a crucial step in the marriage proceedings, validating the suitability of the grooms.
Outcome/Resolution: Vasishta narrates the detailed genealogy of the Ikshvaku dynasty, tracing it from King Aista through a series of powerful and virtuous monarchs, including the miraculous birth of Sagara, down to Dasaratha and his sons, Rama and Lakshmana. This formal presentation of their lineage serves as the basis for Vasishta's request to Janaka for the marriage of his two daughters to the two Ikshvaku princes.

Spiritual_Psychological_Concept_Indian.Concept: Gotra (Lineage/Ancestry - its spiritual purity and importance)
Karma (Action/Consequence - the queen's poisoning act and Sagara's birth)
Daiva (Divine Will/Intervention - Chyavana's blessing for Sagara's birth)
Dharma (Righteousness - the core quality of the Ikshvaku dynasty)

Brief_Summary_Spiritual: Vasishta's narration of the Ikshvaku 'Gotra' (lineage) spiritually validates Rama and Lakshmana for the marriage, emphasizing their descent from a line of 'Dharmic' (righteous) and valorous kings. The story of Sagara's birth, marked by a queen's negative 'Karma' (poisoning) but rectified by 'Daiva' (divine intervention through Chyavana), illustrates how divine grace can overcome adversity within a 'Punya' (meritorious) lineage, ensuring the continuation of a righteous dynasty.
Brief_Summary_Psychological: Psychologically, the narrative reveals the deep-seated anger and jealousy ('intent of destroying the embryo poisoned her') that can arise in familial relationships, leading to destructive acts. King Aista's exile and childlessness would likely induce low mood and hopelessness. The meticulous detailing of the Ikshvaku lineage, culminating in Rama and Lakshmana, serves to bolster their self-esteem and establish their worthiness for the prestigious alliance, reinforcing the psychological importance of a strong, reputable heritage.
